title: Stop the stock lookups from flooding the inventory API

blocks.text: The storefront's `StockClient` used to run its lookups on a pool of 16 platform threads. Since it moved to one virtual thread per lookup, a busy page asks the warehouse's inventory API for hundreds of SKUs at once, and the API, which accepts 6 calls at a time, answers most of them with `429 Too Many Requests`. The storefront then shows "out of stock" for items on the shelf.

Lookups already work. Finish the `TODO` in `src/main/java/practice/StockClient.java`: `callInventory(...)` must never let the API see more than `maxConcurrentCalls` calls in progress, whatever happens to the calls and the threads making them. You may add a field. About six lines in total.

When you're done, the API is never over its limit, SKUs the client already knows are answered straight away even while the API is busy, and a lookup that fails, or whose caller is interrupted, doesn't change how many calls can be in progress.

cases.says: every SKU's stock comes back, from the cache or from the API
the API never has more calls in progress than it accepts, however many lookups run at once
calls that fail leave the limit as it was, so later calls still go through
a SKU the client already knows is answered while the API is busy with other calls
a caller interrupted before its turn does not let an extra call through

origin.section: A Fixed Pool Was Also a Limit: Put a Semaphore in Front of What Is Scarce

concepts: acquire() goes before the try and release() in its finally, so a failed call gives its permit back and an interrupted acquire doesn't release a permit it never took.
The permit is taken around each call to the resource, not around each task, and pooling virtual threads would limit tasks that never touch the resource.
A fixed pool also capped how many tasks reached a scarce resource at once; with one virtual thread per task that cap is gone, and a Semaphore sized to the resource puts it back.
